paragraphs.heading: Gas as moving particles
paragraphs.text: The kinetic theory of gases is a plain, classical model that explains the thermodynamic behaviour of gases. It pictures a gas as a vast number of particles, far too small to see even under a microscope, that never stop moving in random directions. Today we know these particles are the gas's atoms or molecules. Their collisions, with one another and with the walls of the container, explain how volume, pressure and temperature are connected. They also explain the transport properties of a gas: its viscosity, its thermal conductivity and its mass diffusivity.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Bringing in this theory let scientists establish many of the main ideas of thermodynamics. It was the first explicit use of the ideas of statistical mechanics. It is also the theoretical base for rarefied gas dynamics. Its basic version describes an ideal gas.

paragraphs.heading: The ground rules
paragraphs.text: The model assumes the particles are tiny: added together, their own volumes are negligible next to the volume of the container. Put differently, the average gap between particles is large compared with their size. There are so many particles that treating them with statistics is well justified, an assumption sometimes called the thermodynamic limit. The particles keep colliding with one another and with the walls, and every collision is perfectly elastic. Collisions always involve just two particles, never three or more, the particles have no memory, and outside collisions they barely affect each other.

paragraphs.heading: Early hunches
paragraphs.text: Around 50 BC the Roman philosopher Lucretius suggested that objects which seem still are made, on a tiny scale, of fast-moving atoms bouncing off each other. For centuries afterwards, while Aristotle's ideas ruled, this view was rarely taken up. In 1675 Robert Boyle noted that the blow of a hammer turns into motion of the particles inside a nail, and that such motion is what heat is. Around 1760 the Scottish physicist and chemist Joseph Black wrote that many people thought heat was a trembling motion of particles passed from one body to another.

paragraphs.heading: Bernoulli's leap
paragraphs.text: Daniel Bernoulli laid the basis of the theory in his 1738 book Hydrodynamica. He argued that a gas is huge numbers of molecules moving every which way, that their impacts on a surface produce its pressure, and that the average kinetic energy of the molecules sets how hot the gas is. The idea was not accepted at once, partly because the conservation of energy had not yet been established. Physicists also could not see how collisions between molecules could be perfectly elastic. Later pioneers, including Mikhail Lomonosov, John Herapath and John James Waterston, were also largely ignored in their day.

paragraphs.heading: Making it precise
paragraphs.text: In 1856 August Krönig built a simple model that counted only the translational motion of the particles. In 1857 Rudolf Clausius made a more detailed version that also included rotating and vibrating molecules, and he introduced the idea of the mean free path of a particle. In 1859, after reading Clausius, James Clerk Maxwell worked out what share of the molecules move at speeds within any given range. This Maxwell distribution was the first statistical law ever found in physics. In 1871 Ludwig Boltzmann generalised it into the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution.

paragraphs.heading: A turning point
paragraphs.text: As the 20th century began, many physicists still saw atoms as purely imagined constructs rather than real objects. A turning point came with papers on Brownian motion by Albert Einstein in 1905 and Marian Smoluchowski in 1906. Using the kinetic theory, they succeeded in making some accurate predictions in numbers.
